title: Innovation Lightbulb: Non-Resident Patents Are a Sign of U.S. Innovation Strength
gist: Since the late 2000s more than half of new US patents go to non-resident applicants, and the US receives by far the most non-resident patent applications globally; CSIS argues this is a strength, not a vulnerability, because a predictable non-discriminatory IP system attracts foreign firms and know-how needed for reshoring semis, batteries, shipbuilding and robotics.

insights.claim: Since the late 2000s, more than half of all new US patents have been granted to non-resident applicants not primarily domiciled in the United States.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Foreign innovators are deeply invested in US IP protection, a sign of US market centrality.

insights.claim: The United States receives by far the most non-resident patent applications in the world, which signals it is a preferred destination for deploying valuable intellectual assets.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Revealed preference of global innovators supports the US as the hub for technology commercialization.
insights.quote: The United States receives the most non-resident patent applications in the world by far.

insights.claim: Reading high non-resident patent shares as a vulnerability is wrong; protecting foreign IP is reciprocated abroad and US innovators are the world's largest holders of foreign patents, driving a substantial US IP trade surplus.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Policies restricting foreign patentees could invite reciprocal harm to US firms' large overseas IP revenue.

insights.claim: A strong, predictable, non-discriminatory IP system draws foreign innovative firms to invest and partner in the US, and research links non-resident patenting to technology transfer and knowledge spillovers benefiting US firms.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: IP-regime stability is an underappreciated input into FDI flows into US strategic industries.

insights.claim: Reshoring strategic industries such as semiconductor manufacturing, batteries, shipbuilding and robotics depends on attracting foreign firms that hold frontier technology and know-how, making a non-discriminatory IP system a key enabling condition.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Industrial-policy success in these sectors hinges partly on keeping the US IP regime open to foreign players.
